title: CMS Finalizes 2027 Medicare Physician Pay Cut: What Changes for Specialty Practices
summary: CMS finalized a 2.31% Medicare physician pay cut for 2027, deeper than proposed. See what changed, who’s hit hardest and what to do before January 1.
body_markdown:
CMS released its final 2027 Medicare physician fee schedule on November 4, 2026, and the cut came in deeper than proposed. Most specialty practices will be paid 2.31% less per service starting January 1, 2027, up from the 1.68% cut CMS floated in July. Practices have about eight weeks to plan for it.


The rule also changes how Medicare pays for same-day visits and procedures, retires add-on code G2211 and adds new requirements for remote monitoring. Here is what changed, who feels it most and where to look for revenue inside your own operations.


## What CMS finalized


CMS sets two conversion factors: one for clinicians in qualifying advanced alternative payment models (APMs) and one for everyone else. Most specialty practices fall under the lower, non-qualifying factor.


Conversion factor 2026 2027 proposed (July)


2027 final (Nov.) Final change Non-qualifying (most practices)


$33.40 $32.84 $32.63


-2.31% Qualifying APM $33.57


$33.17 $32.95 -1.83%


Most of the decline comes from the expiration of the one-year 2.5% increase Congress provided for 2026 under Public Law 119-21. Statutory updates of +0.25% (non-qualifying) and +0.75% (qualifying) offset part of it.


The cut grew between July and November mostly because of one line item.[CMS's adjustment](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/calendar-year-cy-2027-medicare-physician-fee-schedule-final-rule) for changes to work relative value units (RVUs) moved from +0.53% in the proposal to -0.12% in the final rule. The rule takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.


## The other changes practices will feel


The rate cut gets the headlines, but three billing changes also start Jan. 1.


**Same-day visits and procedures.** When an office visit billed with modifier -25 falls on the same day as a procedure with a 0-day global period, Medicare will pay the higher-paid service in full and the other at 80%. The cut applies when the same physician, or a same-specialty physician in the same group, provides both. CMS scaled this back from July, when it proposed paying the second service at 50% and reaching 10- and 90-day global procedures.


**G2211 becomes modifiers.** Add-on code G2211 for visit complexity is replaced by modifier B1, which raises the visit payment 16%. Clinicians in a Medicare Shared Savings Program ACO or the LEAD Model can use modifier B2 instead, worth 32%. CMS expects minimal overall payment impact, but billing workflows and claim edits need to change before January.


**Remote monitoring.** Remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM) is limited to established patients. Practices billing RTM or remote physiologic monitoring (RPM) must provide a separately billable initiating visit when services begin. A rule requiring employed staff, not contractors, to perform RPM and RTM is delayed to Jan. 1, 2029.


The rule also sets the[end of traditional MIPS reporting](https://www.physicianspractice.com/view/medicare-s-final-2027-fee-schedule-cuts-pay-and-changes-same-day-and-g2211-billing-for-practices) starting with the 2031 performance period, and requires at least one specialty-specific core measure starting in 2027.


## Who feels it most


Independent specialty practices with procedure-heavy schedules take the biggest combined hit.


- **Practices outside advanced APMs** get the full 2.31% cut, not the 1.83% one. That covers most independent specialty groups.
- [Dermatology](https://www.getprosper.ai/outpatient-groups/dermatology) **,**[otolaryngology](https://www.getprosper.ai/outpatient-groups/ent) **and**[podiatry](https://www.getprosper.ai/outpatient-groups/podiatry) face the largest effects from the same-day visit cut, according to CMS. These specialties often pair a visit with a minor procedure.
- **Medicare-heavy specialties** like[ophthalmology](https://www.getprosper.ai/outpatient-groups/ophthalmology) feel the base cut more, because Medicare is a larger share of revenue. Retina practices that bill a visit with a same-day intravitreal injection are also exposed to the -25 cut.
- **Practices billing remote monitoring** need new intake steps before January.


The effect also reaches past Medicare. Many commercial contracts are priced as a percentage of Medicare rates, so a lower fee schedule can pull those payments down too. Your exposure depends on your code mix, payer mix and site of service.


## Why the gap is bigger inside your practice


Practices can't change the conversion factor, but they can control how much revenue they leave on the table. A 2.31% Medicare cut is small next to the leakage most practices already absorb.


Prosper AI's[2026 Growth Report](https://www.getprosper.ai/report/specialty-revenue-growth-2026) estimates an annual opportunity of $125,000 per physician, an 11% revenue increase, from four areas AI can address. The report's[five takeaways](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/top-5-takeaways-specialty-practice-growth-report) summarize each one.

## Four places to look first


**1. Phones.** Prosper AI's CallIQ research, a phone access study of nearly 2,000 specialty practices across 29 states, found 18% of calls go unanswered during office hours, and the after-hours missed-call rate reaches 81%. Among callers who reach someone, 20% wait on hold for more than five minutes. The report values captured demand at $44.8K per physician per year, 36% of the total.


**2. Patients who do not come back.** Per the report, only 54% of patients due for a follow-up visit return on schedule. Prosper AI estimates that re-engaging the rest is worth $37.4K per physician annually, or 30% of the opportunity. Reminders help, but they don’t reach the 6% of patients who never come back on their own. More on that in our guide to[AI voice-enabled patient engagement for specialty practices](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/ai-voice-enabled-patient-engagement) .


**3. Denials.** The report puts the average first-submission denial rate at 10%, rising up to 22% in orthopedics and 16% in gastroenterology. Front-end errors cause about 45% of denials, and the report values fixing them with pre-visit benefit checks at $28.5K per physician per year, 23% of the opportunity. With rates falling, each denied claim costs a larger share of margin, and the new same-day and B1/B2 coding rules add fresh chances for errors in January.


**4. Patient balances.** Per the report, patients pay 36% of the cost of their care on average, and 55% in dermatology. Nearly 8% of what patients owe goes unpaid, and practices collect only 39% of patient balances at the time of service. The report estimates recovering the patient responsibility at $14.1K per physician per year.


## What to do before January 1


1. Rerun your top 20 CPT codes by Medicare volume against the final $32.63 conversion factor (or $32.95 if you qualify through an advanced APM).
2. Pull 12 months of claims with modifier -25 and a 0-day global procedure on the same date. Size what a 20% cut on the lower-paid service means for you.
3. Update billing rules and EHR templates to replace G2211 with modifier B1 (or B2 for eligible ACO clinicians).
4. If you bill RPM or RTM, add the required initiating visit to your intake workflow.
5. Measure your office-hours and after-hours[missed-call rates](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/missed-calls-specialty-practices) . Without a baseline, you can't size the gap.
6. Break out first-submission denial rates by payer and specialty, and compare them with the 10% average in Prosper AI's report.
7. Review how patient balances are estimated, communicated and collected before the visit.


8. Run your numbers through the[revenue growth calculator](https://www.getprosper.ai/practice-revenue-growth-calculator) to see which lever is largest for your specialty.


Prosper AI's opportunity estimates are averages across specialty practices and will differ for your practice.
